title: Montana

jokes.text: He's hung like a field mouse. I mean, you pop the diaper and... boing! It's like a little sundial.
jokes.setup: Robin Williams is talking warmly about his new baby
jokes.punchline: Pivots immediately to the baby's tiny genitalia, comparing it to a sundial
jokes.explanation: Robin Williams doing his signature riff on new-parenthood — the 'field mouse' simile is unexpected and vivid, and 'little sundial' escalates brilliantly. Feels genuinely improvised-but-sharp. High character integration because only Robin Williams would land this in this register. Loses a little for being a talk-show guest bit rather than tightly structured sitcom writing.

dialogue.speaker: Robin Williams
dialogue.line: He's wonderful. I mean, he's hung like a field mouse.

jokes.text: 'Honey, what time is it?' 'Get the baby. Get the baby.' 'Look! It's 3:00! Oh, it's 2:30 now. It's real cold.'
jokes.setup: The sundial joke established the baby's small genitalia as a comic premise
jokes.punchline: Williams acts out a couple using it as an actual clock, with the temperature-shrinkage detail ('it's real cold') as the kicker
jokes.explanation: This is the escalation payoff on the sundial setup and it's genuinely excellent — acting out the couple using the baby as a timepiece is absurdist but internally logical, and the cold-temperature shrinkage detail ('it's 2:30 now') is a perfectly timed physical-comedy kicker delivered verbally. Strong Williams character integration. Earns its 8+ because the comedic logic is airtight and the image is indelible.

dialogue.speaker: Robin Williams
dialogue.line: I mean, you pop the diaper and... boing! It's like a little sundial.

jokes.text: Baby ca-ca is like kryptonite for the father. Even the dog looks at me like, 'you don't put his face in it.'
jokes.setup: Williams pivots from genitalia jokes to the shared horror of diaper duty
jokes.punchline: The dog's judging look implies a dog's normal diaper-face behavior is something even the dog won't endorse on the baby
jokes.explanation: Competent Williams riff — the kryptonite metaphor is workable and the dog's implied moral superiority is a nice twist, but it's a somewhat familiar 'dads hate diapers' territory. Mid-range, well-executed but not special.

dialogue.speaker: Robin Williams
dialogue.line: Honey, what time is it? Get the baby. Get the baby. Look! It's 3:00! Oh, it's 2:30 now. It's real cold.

jokes.text: He has his own little credit card called 'Fetal Express.'
jokes.setup: Observation that the baby is growing up fast
jokes.punchline: 'Fetal Express' — a punning parody of American Express applied to an infant
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical wordplay — 'Fetal Express' is the kind of tight coinage that stands alone. The joke is fully contained in three words. High economy score because there's no fat on it. Quotability is high.

dialogue.speaker: Robin Williams
dialogue.line: It is like kryptonite for... for the father. Even the dog looks at me like, 'you don't put his face in it.'

jokes.text: He's dialing up one of those '976-suckle,' you know? I'm waiting for you. I'm lactating. Call me.
jokes.setup: The baby's grown-up credit card premise leads to adult phone-line parody
jokes.punchline: '976-suckle' — a 900-number parody for nursing, with the lactating seductive voice bit
jokes.explanation: '976-suckle' is another tight coinage in the same vein as 'Fetal Express,' and the seductive lactation voice adds a pleasingly transgressive layer. Firmly Williams-coded humor. Good escalation within the bit.

dialogue.speaker: Robin Williams
dialogue.line: It's almost like I know that he's growing old because he's, like, he's 8 months and he has his own little credit card called 'fetal express.'

jokes.text: Larry: 'I like the kryptonite suit.' Robin: 'What is it, is it Japanese?' Larry: 'It is.' Robin: 'And what is this? This is Sears, right?' Larry: 'Yes, so they're both Japanese.'
jokes.setup: Williams compliments Larry's suit; Larry deflects credit by pointing to Sears
jokes.punchline: Williams immediately equates Japanese fashion with Sears — an absurd non-sequitur that Larry plays completely straight with his deadpan agreement
jokes.explanation: A mild, absurdist non-sequitur that works because of Larry's deadpan delivery. The logic is knowingly broken but the joke doesn't quite transcend its 'off-the-cuff celebrity chat' framing. Functional, pleasant.

dialogue.speaker: Robin Williams
dialogue.line: He's dialing up one of those '976-suckle,' you know? I'm waiting for you. I'm lactating. Call me.

jokes.text: Artie: 'It's a magpie. They're scavengers — feed on road kill, dead meat. They carry rabies and Lyme disease. You better not take a nap on your porch. They'll peck your eyes out.' Larry: 'Still. Every day.'
jokes.setup: Artie demolishes Larry's cherished bird fantasy with a clinical list of terrors
jokes.punchline: Larry's response — 'Still. Every day.' — refuses to process any of it
jokes.explanation: This is the standout comedic moment of the episode. 'Still. Every day.' is a masterclass in comedic economy — three words that perfectly encapsulate Larry's character (narcissistic self-delusion, reality-resistance) and land as pure deadpan. The setup is Artie's escalating list of horrors (rabies, Lyme disease, eye-pecking), each funnier than the last, and Larry's complete refusal to update his worldview is the perfect non-sequitur button. This is what the show does better than almost anyone: the funniest moment is the quietest one. Earns 8+ because it's character-specific, structurally perfect, and deeply quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: I think I like the kryptonite suit. That's actually what it seems like.

jokes.text: Larry reveals he watched the tapes of his old show and says 'I've never been so miserable in my life' — implying he hated watching himself
jokes.setup: Artie mentions he saw 'the complete years of the Larry Sanders Show' — the tapes in the closet
jokes.punchline: Larry's response is that watching the show made him miserable, the opposite of what you'd expect from a narcissist reviewing his own legacy
jokes.explanation: A nice character-comedy beat — the reveal that Larry watched his own tapes and was miserable (rather than narcissistically pleased) is a good subversion, and it sets up the plot. Functional, character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: What is it, is it Japanese?
It is.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: And what is this?
This is sears, right?

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Yes, so they're both Japanese.
OK.

jokes.text: 'You're a talk show animal. You're like one of those goddamn creatures out of Greek mythology — half man, half desk.'
jokes.setup: Artie is urging Larry to come back, saying he was never made for Montana
jokes.punchline: The mythological creature analogy lands on 'half man, half desk' — a perfectly absurdist image that is also deeply true about Larry
jokes.explanation: The best written joke in the episode. 'Half man, half desk' is a genuine piece of comedy writing genius — it perfectly satirizes the late-night host as a creature inseparable from his format, uses Greek mythology as an unexpected register that makes the absurdity land harder, and is so economically structured that nothing could be added or removed. It's also deeply character-specific: this exact description could only apply to Larry Sanders in this world. The joke also works as a thesis statement for the entire series. Easily earns 9+.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You hear that? That's my whippoorwill, Artie.

jokes.text: 'Get off the porch, asshole.' (Larry to a bird, immediately after Artie's speech)
jokes.setup: Artie has just delivered a serious, emotional speech about Larry being a 'talk show animal'
jokes.punchline: Larry deflects the weight of the moment by shouting at the disease-carrying bird (the magpie) on his porch
jokes.explanation: A magnificent callback and reaction beat. The emotional weight of 'half man, half desk' is instantly punctured by Larry shouting 'Get off the porch, asshole' at the magpie — which ties back to the earlier bird running gag. It's funny on its own, funnier as a callback, and it also characterizes Larry's emotional avoidance perfectly. The economy is near-perfect: five words that do triple duty (laugh, callback, character beat). Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, Larry, it's a magpie. They're scavengers, you know? They feed on road kill, dead meat. You know they carry rabies and lyme disease? You better not take a nap out on your porch. They'll peck your eyes out.

jokes.text: Larry: 'That's pathetic. We should save that one for when I really have a drug problem, don't you think?'
jokes.setup: Artie suggests they claim Larry had a drug problem to explain his disappearance
jokes.punchline: Larry dismisses it as 'pathetic' — but says they should save it for a real drug problem, implying he expects to have one
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly dark line — the funniest thing about it is the casual resignation in 'when I really have a drug problem.' The irony is rich (he ends up using the cover story anyway in this very episode), and the line is deeply character-specific: Larry's self-awareness about his own psychological trajectory is a key part of what makes him tragic-funny. Earns 8+ for its economy, dark wit, and the dramatic irony it establishes.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Still. Every day.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I didn't want you to see me, so I flew coach. I don't know how people do it. They don't even give you those little wet towels. I had to wipe my face with a pack of Sweet'N Low.'
jokes.setup: Larry catches Artie having followed him on the same flight to Montana
jokes.punchline: Artie's complaint about coach is perfectly in character — a man of a certain era completely undone by the indignity of not getting a hot towel
jokes.explanation: The specific detail of wiping his face with a Sweet'N Low packet is wonderfully precise and character-specific for Artie — a man of old Hollywood standards forced into the economy of normal life. 'I don't know how people do it' is the perfect Artie register.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You're like one of those goddamn creatures out of Greek mythology... half man, half desk.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I can't believe Leno actually hid in the closet so he could hear the whole network meeting. That's a sickness, to be so obsessed with what people are saying about you.' [beat] 'What did people say about me not being mentioned much in the book?'
jokes.setup: Larry is disparaging Jay Leno for obsessive, insecure behavior he read about in a book
jokes.punchline: Immediately asks what people said about HIM not being mentioned — doing the exact same thing he just mocked
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect ironic self-own. The joke's architecture is textbook: set up the hypocrisy with a confident moral statement, then immediately collapse it. But what elevates this above a standard hypocrisy joke is (a) the Leno reference grounds it in real industry jealousy, (b) the specific detail that Larry is upset about NOT being mentioned (so even his insecurity is about being ignored, not criticized), and (c) the complete lack of self-awareness in the delivery. This is the show at its best — character comedy that also functions as industry satire. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Get off the porch, asshole.

jokes.text: Hank on the lottery show: 'Tonight's super-spin jackpot is up to $3 million, which means a lot of pesos for some very lucky winner. And by pesos I don't mean to imply that someone of Hispanic descent is likely to win. Again.'
jokes.setup: Hank is hosting a lottery show — a humiliating comedown from the Larry Sanders Show
jokes.punchline: 'And by pesos I don't mean to imply that someone of Hispanic descent is likely to win. Again.' — the word 'Again' reveals this has happened before and Hank has been corrected for it
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best constructed jokes. 'Again' is doing enormous comedic work — it implies Hank has made this exact gaffe before, has been disciplined for it, and is now attempting a correction that itself proves he hasn't learned anything. It's simultaneously character comedy (Hank's oblivious racism-adjacent blundering), cringe comedy, and a perfect example of comedic economy. The joke would be good without 'Again'; with it, it's excellent. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Or we could say you had a drug problem. You had to hide out in montana till you dried out. I tell you, that's the only surefire way I know of avoiding embarrassment.

jokes.text: Hank says 'say now' instead of 'hey, now' to draw the lottery number
jokes.setup: Hank can't say 'hey, now' — his signature catchphrase — because it's the intellectual property of the Larry Sanders Show
jokes.punchline: 'Say now' is a pathetic, legally-safe substitute that makes him sound ridiculous
jokes.explanation: A beautifully sad and funny piece of character comedy. Hank's identity is so bound up in his catchphrase that being legally barred from it reduces him to 'say now' — a meaningless syllable substitution. The joke also illustrates the intellectual poverty of the catchphrase itself: it has no content, it's just a sound Hank makes. Deep character integration, good structure, and the setup/punchline ('Well, he can't say hey now — that's the intellectual property of the Larry Sanders Show') is sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's pathetic. We should save that one for when I really have a drug problem, don't you think?

jokes.text: Larry: 'What about "no flipping"?' Artie: 'Public domain. Sorry.'
jokes.setup: They've been discussing Hank's catchphrase being IP-protected; Larry asks about his own signature 'no flipping'
jokes.punchline: Artie casually informs Larry that 'no flipping' is public domain — Larry's signature bit is worthless
jokes.explanation: Sharp economy — 'Public domain. Sorry.' is three words that simultaneously deflate Larry's ego and deliver a legal-comedy punchline. The joke works because it treats showbiz IP law as both real and absurd. Artie's 'Sorry' is perfectly calibrated deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I love these fuckers.

jokes.text: Yeah. I'm just gonna start assembling the staff tomorrow. / What did I just say? Low profile. / Fine.
jokes.setup: Artie has just told Larry to keep a low profile while he negotiates
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately announces he's going to do the opposite; Artie catches him; Larry capitulates in one word
jokes.explanation: A clean comedic beat that efficiently establishes Larry's inability to follow instructions and Artie's exasperated authority. The 'Fine' capitulation is good but not exceptional. Works as a character moment rather than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: They don't even give you those little towels, those little wet towels. I had to wipe my face with a pack of sweet'n low.

jokes.text: Beverly reveals she started smoking the night Larry left, and Larry asks to crack the window — which doesn't work
jokes.setup: Larry visits Beverly (his assistant) in the car, trying to quietly recruit her back
jokes.punchline: The car is full of smoke, the window is broken — a small, perfect portrait of a world that fell apart when Larry left
jokes.explanation: A quiet, cringe-comedy beat — the detail of Beverly chain-smoking since Larry left and the broken window trapping them together is good observational character comedy. Not a big laugh but contributes to the episode's cumulative portrait of Larry's absence as minor apocalypse.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Man, I can't believe Leno actually hid in the closet so he could hear the whole network meeting. That's a sickness, to be so obsessed with what people are saying about you.

jokes.text: 'Looks like a goddamn Cheech and Chong movie.' Larry: 'That's not a bad booking idea, Artie. Cheech and Chong.'
jokes.setup: Artie complains about two grown men sitting in a car full of smoke
jokes.punchline: Larry, incapable of being present for any human moment, immediately converts the Cheech and Chong reference into a booking idea
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy. Larry's brain is so irreversibly wired for the show that a complaint about smoke instantly becomes a guest booking idea. It's funny, it's sad, it's a great encapsulation of the 'half man, half desk' thesis. The joke earns its high character integration score because this could ONLY be Larry Sanders.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I know. That is a sickness. What did people say about me not being mentioned much in the book?

jokes.text: Artie: 'The show was all he had, Larry. At least, thank God, I have a skill.'
jokes.setup: Artie is describing how Hank was devastated by the show ending
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'skill' is calling lottery numbers — the joke is that this is presented with total dignity as a genuine alternative career
jokes.explanation: A quietly funny self-serving delusion — Artie presenting lottery hosting as a 'skill' with complete sincerity. Works because Artie is normally the show's wisest character; the small vanity is endearing and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And by pesos I don't mean to imply that someone of hispanic descent is likely to win. Again.

jokes.text: Larry: 'A free scratcher ticket?' [in response to what the lottery people give Hank as respect]
jokes.setup: Hank says the lottery people give him something Larry can't — respect. Pause.
jokes.punchline: Larry guesses 'a free scratcher ticket' — which is funnier than the real answer ('respect') and perfectly undercuts the dignity Hank was reaching for
jokes.explanation: A perfectly timed misdirection beat. The audience (and Larry) both expect 'respect' or something heartfelt; 'a free scratcher ticket' is the comedically correct wrong answer that's funnier than the real one. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: 'Say now'? Say now. Well, he can't say 'hey, now.' That's the intellectual property of the Larry Sanders show.

jokes.text: Larry is conducting a secret staff-reassembly meeting with Darlene in the dark on the empty stage
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to maintain 'low profile' while secretly reassembling his staff
jokes.punchline: He's meeting people one by one in the dark on his old stage — furtive, absurd, and a pure visual gag
jokes.explanation: A good visual/situational gag — the whole 'low profile' operation conducted in a conspicuously theatrical fashion. The physical staging (dark stage, furtive meetings) is funny and consistent with Larry's absurd self-awareness blindspot.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You really pulled the rug out from under me, Larry boy.

jokes.text: Darlene: 'Working for Hank was the most meaningful experience of my life.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to recruit Darlene back to his show
jokes.punchline: She describes working for Hank — a lottery show host — as the most meaningful experience of her life, a devastating commentary on both Hank and her own life
jokes.explanation: A beautifully deflating line — the sincerity with which she says it makes it funnier. It's an indictment of both the smallness of Hank's world and the comedy of his delusion about his own importance.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You had it on 'passenger window lock.'

jokes.text: Larry's confessional recruiting speech: 'I know that in the past I've been difficult to work for.' Beverly: 'Um-hum.' 'Insensitive.' 'Um-hum.' 'Disorganized.' 'Um-hum.' 'I know you don't feel that way.' [Beverly has been agreeing to all the bad things]
jokes.setup: Larry is making a heartfelt recruiting speech listing his flaws, expecting Beverly to reassure him
jokes.punchline: Beverly has been sincerely agreeing with every flaw — and Larry's pivot to 'I know you don't feel that way' reveals he didn't notice
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured cringe escalation. Each 'Um-hum' is funnier than the last as the audience realizes Beverly is genuinely agreeing with every indictment, and the kicker — Larry's cheerful 'I know you don't feel that way' — is perfect because he has completely failed to process what just happened. Strong character integration for both characters: Larry's narcissistic self-unawareness and Beverly's quiet, long-suffering honesty.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Is this what you call low profile? Two grown men sitting in a car full of smoke? Looks like a goddamn cheech and chong movie.

jokes.text: The janitor Don interrupts the secret meeting: 'Excuse me, Mr. Sanders. Are you going to be having any more secret meetings today or can I lock up the stage now?'
jokes.setup: Larry is conducting furtive, supposedly secret meetings in the dark on his old stage
jokes.punchline: The janitor has clearly been watching the whole parade of secret meetings and names them as such without ceremony
jokes.explanation: A perfectly dry line — the janitor's complete lack of deference to Larry's theater of secrecy is very funny, especially the implication that there have been multiple secret meetings and Don has been patiently waiting. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: A free scratcher ticket?

jokes.text: Larry's assistant reveals she was never fired — she's still been getting a paycheck every week
jokes.setup: Larry has prepared an elaborate emotional speech about needing her back
jokes.punchline: She was never fired — his business manager has been paying her all along — making the whole speech unnecessary
jokes.explanation: A solid setup/punchline that deflates Larry's grand gesture retroactively. The comedy is in how much emotional preparation was wasted on nothing. Character-specific and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: They give me respect.

jokes.text: Larry's writer reveals Conan O'Brien offered him a job as associate producer — 'very involved in the creative direction.' Larry: 'How long do you think that's gonna stay on the air?'
jokes.setup: Phil (writer) has a competing offer from Conan O'Brien's show
jokes.punchline: Larry questions Conan's longevity — the joke works on two levels: Larry's petty competitiveness and the historical irony of Conan's actual NBC fate
jokes.explanation: An industry-insider joke that gains enormous rewatch value given Conan's eventual NBC cancellation. In 1994 (early Conan era), this reads as petty Larry jealousy; in retrospect, it's accidentally prophetic. The character integration is excellent — this is exactly how Larry would handle a competing offer.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm trying to keep this very low profile, darlene.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I'll see you Monday.' Phil: 'So what have you been up to the last 3 months, Phil?' Larry: 'Oh, jerking off. See you Monday.'
jokes.setup: Larry has secured Phil's return with a dismissive 'See you Monday'; he then offers a pro forma 'how've you been'
jokes.punchline: Phil's answer is 'jerking off' — delivered with such frank brevity that it becomes both funny and a bit sad
jokes.explanation: An extremely economical joke — the brevity and honesty of 'jerking off' lands perfectly after the series of formal meetings. The 'See you Monday' button that follows it mirrors Larry's earlier 'See you Monday,' creating a tiny satisfying structural echo. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: But you never fired me.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I didn't?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: No. Your business manager gives me a paycheck every week.

jokes.text: Larry's emotional speech to someone (implied to be his dog): 'Don't speak. Just listen... I need to know that no matter what happens, you will never abandon me like that again. I need to hear you promise me.' [pause] 'OK. That's good enough for me. I am back.'
jokes.setup: Larry launches into an emotional, desperate speech — the audience assumes it's to a person
jokes.punchline: The 'promise' is implied to come from his dog (who cannot speak), and Larry accepts a silent pause as sufficient commitment
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed misdirection sequence. The audience is allowed to think this is a meaningful human reconnection; the reveal that it's a dog (and that Larry accepts non-verbal dog-silence as a binding promise) is both funny and a perfect character beat. It also works on a meta level — Larry Sanders' most honest emotional relationship is with his dog. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: So what have you been up to the last 3 months, Phil?

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Oh, jerking off. See you Monday.

jokes.text: Artie: 'This would have been the perfect time to get rid of some of the deadwood in the office.' Larry: 'Oh, you mean Paula?' Artie: 'I'm not saying, but some of these people are useless. They should be cut out of here like cancer.'
jokes.setup: Larry has hired the entire staff back; Artie is unhappy
jokes.punchline: Artie's genteel refusal to name names while clearly having a hit list is funny; his pivot to the cancer metaphor escalates the hostility absurdly
jokes.explanation: A competent character beat — Artie's barely concealed contempt for some staff members and his cancer metaphor are in character and mildly funny. Doesn't rise above functional.

dialogue.speaker: Arthur
dialogue.line: I need to hear you promise me that.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: (Larry says nothing)

jokes.text: I can't believe you hired the entire staff back. / No, this would have been the perfect time to get rid of some of the deadwood in the office.
jokes.setup: Artie is annoyed Larry reassembled the whole staff
jokes.punchline: Artie, who has been entirely focused on getting Larry his dignity back, reveals he also wanted to use the opportunity to purge staff — pure Hollywood pragmatism
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat for Artie but not particularly original. Works as a moment that reveals Artie's ruthless pragmatism beneath his loyalty. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Oh, God. It's good to know I'll never have to pull another set of balls like that again.

jokes.text: Hank bursts in: 'Hello, children! Look at you! All back where you belong. Aw, it does my heart good. The whole family is here!' Artie: 'What, are you gonna start singing?'
jokes.setup: Everyone is reuniting backstage; Hank makes his grand entrance
jokes.punchline: Artie's deflating 'What, are you gonna start singing?' is the perfect straight-man response to Hank's theatrical warmth
jokes.explanation: A good dynamic beat between Hank's theatrical warmth and Artie's bone-dry deflationary wit. Both characters are perfectly themselves here.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: They should be cut out of here like cancer.

jokes.text: Hello, children! Look at you! All back where you belong. Aw, it does my heart good. Ah, the whole family is here.
jokes.setup: Hank walks into the show and sees the assembled staff
jokes.punchline: Hank's performance of magnanimous patriarch ('children,' 'whole family') is absurd given that he was also just coerced back, also does a lottery show, and also has zero authority here
jokes.explanation: Pure Hank — the grandiosity is completely unearned and he knows it, but he commits fully. 'Are you gonna start singing?' from Artie is the right puncture. Character consistent but not particularly inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Germain
dialogue.line: Larry walked, I put on back-to-back cheers reruns in the spot and they're doing rather well. Better then Leno as a matter of fact.

jokes.text: The network exec (Germain) walks in just as Larry and Artie are making their move — 'Gentlemen, you take me by surprise. I must say that I'm not prepared to put the show back on.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie have come to the network to force the show back on the air
jokes.punchline: Germain simply... doesn't want to. The whole scheme immediately begins to collapse.
jokes.explanation: A solid situational comedic beat — the plan immediately hitting a wall is funny, and Germain's polite intractability sets up the episode's best satirical passage.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: If you say you're gonna sue somebody, the least you can do is follow through and sue them.

jokes.text: Germain: 'Larry walked, I put on back-to-back Cheers reruns and they're doing rather well. Better than Leno, as a matter of fact.'
jokes.setup: Larry expects the network desperately needs him back
jokes.punchline: Cheers reruns are outperforming Leno — the entire premise of Larry's indispensability collapses
jokes.explanation: A sharp industry-satire joke — the implication that old sitcom reruns outperform a real late-night host is darkly funny and rings true. The Leno dig adds insider flavor.

dialogue.speaker: Germain
dialogue.line: Oh, please, don't tell me you and Larry are lovers.

jokes.text: Larry: 'This is bullshit. This reminds me why I hate the fucking business. If you say you're gonna sue somebody, the least you can do is follow through and sue them. I'm going back to Montana.'
jokes.setup: The network drops the lawsuit — the plan that was supposed to restore Larry's dignity falls apart
jokes.punchline: Larry's outrage is directed at the network's failure to follow through on SUING him — he wanted to be sued
jokes.explanation: An excellent absurdist character outburst. The comedy is in the inversion — Larry is outraged that the network WON'T sue him, because the lawsuit was supposed to give him dignity. The logic is twisted but internally coherent, and the righteous fury with which Larry defends his right to be sued is pure character comedy gold. 'The least you can do is follow through and sue them' is a brilliant line. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Germain
dialogue.line: Something about the dynamic?

jokes.text: Artie: 'Now, listen, nobody knows about th—' Germain: 'Oh please, don't tell me you and Larry are lovers.' Artie: 'No, of course not.' [pause] 'Now, listen—' Germain: 'What could make you think we're lovers?!'
jokes.setup: Artie begins a secretive setup for a big reveal
jokes.punchline: Germain's preemptive guess — 'you and Larry are lovers' — derails everything; and then the delayed reaction of Artie getting flustered about why that might be assumed is a perfect second beat
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured two-beat joke. The first beat (Germain's guess) is a good misdirection; the second beat — Artie's delayed, offended 'What could make you think we're lovers?!' — is the real laugh because it reveals Artie is more troubled by the plausibility of the suggestion than by the inappropriateness of the question. Germain's 'Something about the dynamic?' is the perfect needle. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Germain
dialogue.line: Well, that explains a lot... the mood swings, the attention disorder, the astonishing weight gain.

jokes.text: Germain: 'Something about the dynamic?'
jokes.setup: Artie has just indignantly demanded to know what could make Germain think he and Larry are lovers
jokes.punchline: 'Something about the dynamic?' — three words delivered with complete composure that simultaneously explain nothing and everything
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum comedy. 'Something about the dynamic?' is perfectly calibrated — it's not an insult, it's not an explanation, it's a polite observation that somehow lands as both. The economy score is as high as it gets: nothing could be added or removed. This is the kind of line comedy writers go home happy about.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He's as clean as Louie Anderson's dinner plate.

jokes.text: Germain: 'Well, that explains a lot... the mood swings, the attention disorder, the astonishing weight gain.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just revealed Larry had a drug problem
jokes.punchline: Germain accepts it completely and adds 'the astonishing weight gain' — the most cutting detail — with casual brutality
jokes.explanation: The escalating list works because each item is plausible, but 'astonishing weight gain' is the unexpected kicker — it's crueler than the clinical terms before it and sounds like something Germain has been quietly thinking for a while. The word 'astonishing' is doing extra work.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I didn't hear it ring. Oh, it didn't. It's a new system. You see, there's a little flashing light here you can't see from where you're standing.

jokes.text: 'He's as clean as Louie Anderson's dinner plate.'
jokes.setup: Germain asks 'Is he clean?' about Larry's drug recovery
jokes.punchline: Artie's simile — 'clean as Louie Anderson's dinner plate' — implies Louie Anderson eats everything, so his plate is spotlessly clean. It's simultaneously a weight joke and a weird compliment.
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest one-liners in the episode. The joke works on multiple levels: it's a 'clean' simile that functions as a fat joke (Louie Anderson doesn't leave food on his plate), but it's also such a specific and unexpected reference that it takes a beat to land — which is part of what makes it brilliant. The simile is structurally airtight, the economy is near-perfect, and it's deeply in Artie's voice (old Hollywood casual cruelty disguised as a figure of speech). Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Germain
dialogue.line: Where's the gent's?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Uh, right out the door, first crapper on the left.

jokes.text: Artie pretends to receive a phone call on a phone that didn't ring; when Germain calls it out, Artie claims there's a new system with a flashing light Germain can't see from where he's standing
jokes.setup: Larry has appeared in the hallway; Artie needs to get Germain out of the room
jokes.punchline: The phantom phone call — Artie's desperate improvised lie and Germain's immediate skepticism
jokes.explanation: A functional cringe-comedy moment — Artie's frantic improvisation under pressure and Germain's calm, observational 'I didn't hear it ring' are a good double act. The 'flashing light you can't see from where you're standing' is a nice specific lie.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What'd he mean by astonishing weight gain?

jokes.text: Artie directs Germain to the bathroom: 'Right out the door, first crapper on the left. Enjoy.'
jokes.setup: Artie needs to get rid of Germain while Larry is in the hallway
jokes.punchline: 'First crapper on the left. Enjoy.' — the word 'crapper' in a corporate setting and the surreal 'Enjoy' make this funny
jokes.explanation: Artie's vocabulary — 'crapper' — and the absurd hospitality of 'Enjoy' in the context of directing someone to a toilet makes this a small, perfectly delivered laugh. Economy is high.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Never mind that. What about the gay lovers thing?

jokes.text: Larry appears in the hallway — Artie panics and hisses at him while trying to control the situation
jokes.setup: Artie is desperately trying to keep Larry hidden while managing Germain
jokes.punchline: The frantic hustle — including 'Vamanos! Andalay! Pronto!' — is pure physical farce disguised as a quiet hallway scene
jokes.explanation: A comedic setpiece that works primarily through performance — the 'Vamanos! Andalay! Pronto!' from Artie is a funny escalation, even if the broader scene is more plot than comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: ¡vamanos! ¡andalay! ¡pronto!

jokes.text: Larry, hearing the network will give him the show back, asks: 'What did he mean by astonishing weight gain?'
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to convey the great news that they got the show back
jokes.punchline: Larry's only concern is the 'astonishing weight gain' comment — his vanity completely overrides his relief
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback and character beat. The stakes should be enormous — Larry is getting his show back — but his only response is wounded vanity about the weight comment. This is pitch-perfect Larry Sanders characterization: narcissism as a force that distorts all proportion. High character integration, excellent economy, and the rewatch bonus is earned because knowing Germain said it offscreen makes the callback funnier.

dialogue.line: He hasn't changed.

jokes.text: Larry: 'What about the gay lovers thing?' [same priority as the weight gain concern]
jokes.setup: Larry has just asked about the weight gain comment; he pivots to equal concern about the gay lovers implication
jokes.punchline: Both the weight and the sexuality speculation are treated with identical urgency — all that matters is Larry's image
jokes.explanation: A good secondary callback — Larry's vanity extends to both the weight and the sexuality implication being equally concerning to him. The comedy is in the equivalence he places on them.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I had a... ahem... an addiction to painkillers.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Trust me.' Larry: 'That's a last resort?' Artie: 'Last resort.' Larry: 'You could've come up with something a little less pathetic.' Artie: 'Just calm down. Take one of these.' [hands Larry a pill]
jokes.setup: Larry is furious that Artie invented a drug problem to explain his absence
jokes.punchline: Artie soothes Larry's anger about a fake drug problem by literally handing him a pill
jokes.explanation: A spectacular piece of dark comedy. The irony is complete and perfect: Larry is enraged that Artie INVENTED a drug problem for him, and Artie's solution is to immediately give him actual pills to calm down. The fact that Larry takes them without hesitation makes it even darker and funnier. This is the episode's sharpest constructed ironic payoff. Earns 8+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, she got that because that's how they're wearing it in prison.

jokes.text: Artie pushing the pills back and forth with Larry — 'Take them. Take them. Take them.' / 'No, you take them.' — escalating into a farcical pill-passing standoff
jokes.setup: Artie has given Larry pills; Larry tries to give them back
jokes.punchline: The mutual refusal to hold the pills becomes a physical comedy escalation that mirrors their codependency
jokes.explanation: A decent physical comedy escalation that extends the dark pill-passing joke. The back-and-forth is funny but loses some momentum — the best version of this joke was joke #46.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I actually saw a hooker dressed in a barney outfit. It was unbelievable. Now when barney sings, 'you love me, I love you,' it costs you 250 bucks.

jokes.text: Yeah, yeah. Oh, Bernadette. Hi! So good to see you... Did Artie talk to you about maybe singing the 'hello, Larry' kind of song to me? / Yeah, yeah. / Oh, good, good, good.
jokes.setup: Bernadette Peters is meeting Larry before the show; Larry asks if Artie talked to her about a welcome-back song
jokes.punchline: Larry has apparently already arranged with Artie to have Bernadette perform a personal tribute to him — an astonishing level of self-congratulation pre-arranged for his first night back
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Larry's assumption that this is an appropriate request — arranging your own tribute performance from a guest. Pure Larry Sanders self-involvement. Sets up the awkward back-and-forth that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Larry comes out and he tells the people that he was molested as a child. All right? Of course, I mean we have people who call your parents and we tell them we're just making it up.

jokes.text: Bernadette Peters refuses to sing Larry's 'welcome back' song because 'when Bette Midler sang goodbye to Johnny on his last show...' — comparing Larry's situation unfavorably
jokes.setup: Larry wants Bernadette Peters to sing a 'welcome back' song on his first night
jokes.punchline: She invokes the Bette Midler/Johnny Carson farewell as a comparison point — implying an ending is more meaningful than a return — and Larry has to fight for it while pretending not to care
jokes.explanation: A good cringe-comedy exchange — Larry's desperation for validation and his simultaneous pretense of not needing it is the show's signature emotional register. The Carson/Bette Midler reference grounds it in real late-night mythology.

dialogue.speaker: Bernadette Peters
dialogue.line: And every night, I say a prayer, thank the lord, Hank Kingsley's back!

jokes.text: Larry: 'But I have — I have something special planned.' 'Should I tell the band, because they'll need to know the key.' [Bernadette insists she's not singing] Larry: 'How's your mother?'
jokes.setup: Larry keeps barreling through social cues, trying to lock in the song
jokes.punchline: 'How's your mother?' — a complete non-sequitur that signals Larry has given up and reverted to desperate small talk
jokes.explanation: 'How's your mother?' is a perfect comedic escape hatch — three words that simultaneously admit defeat, change the subject, and reveal Larry's complete social mechanism breakdown. The economy is near-perfect and it's deeply in the show's register of awkward social maneuvering.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Thank the lord, Hank Kingsley's back!

jokes.text: Bernadette: 'He hasn't changed.' [to camera/crew, as Larry rushes off]
jokes.setup: Larry has just bounced between desperation and dismissal in the space of thirty seconds
jokes.punchline: 'He hasn't changed.' — delivered to someone offscreen with a knowing smile
jokes.explanation: A good reaction beat — understated and efficient. 'He hasn't changed' works as both a laugh and an episode thesis statement.

jokes.text: Artie finds Larry attempting to meditate/find his aura backstage and asks to join him. Larry: 'Fine.' They both sit in silence.
jokes.setup: Pre-show nerves; Larry is doing something spiritually incongruous
jokes.punchline: Artie joins him without ceremony; neither says anything meaningful; the silence is the joke
jokes.explanation: A quiet, warm comedic beat — the implicit tenderness of Artie silently joining Larry's neurotic pre-show ritual is more sweet than funny, but it works as character comedy in the show's specific register.

jokes.text: Hank cannot get 'Live on tape' right — keeps flubbing it in the green room with staff reassuring him
jokes.setup: Hank is getting ready to go back on air as Larry's sidekick
jokes.punchline: He can't say the three-word phrase correctly — the simplest possible job — suggesting total psychological breakdown from his time away
jokes.explanation: A good running comedy of Hank's anxiety — 'live on tape' is both funny in itself (as a contradictory phrase) and as a vehicle for showing Hank's fragility. His repeated failure at this simple task escalates nicely.

jokes.text: I'm not going out there. / You haven't got a choice. / I'm not going out there. / I am not going out there.
jokes.setup: Larry has learned the humiliating terms of his return (publicly admitting a fake drug addiction on air)
jokes.punchline: Larry's escalating refusals — three variations of 'not going out there' — each more emphatic and less convincing than the last
jokes.explanation: Standard cringe escalation — the repeated denial that clearly will not hold. Functional but the joke is the situation rather than any particular line. The comedy lands through context (we know he's going out there).

jokes.text: Hank: 'I'm not going out there.' [repeated multiple times, with increasing petulance] Artie: 'You don't like it, go back to that cabin and do a show on public access.'
jokes.setup: Hank is refusing to go on stage and face humiliation
jokes.punchline: Artie's threat of 'public access' as the alternative is perfectly calibrated to Hank's ego — the worst possible fate
jokes.explanation: Artie weaponizing 'public access' against Hank's showbiz vanity is a perfectly targeted line. 'Public access' is the ultimate insult in this world.

jokes.text: The audience carries Larry onto the stage like a conquering hero — Larry awkwardly receives this as normal while looking mortified
jokes.setup: Larry refused to go out; the show needed him on stage
jokes.punchline: He is physically carried/ushered out — 'Down you go. Down you go.' — a deeply undignified entry for a man whose dignity is everything
jokes.explanation: A good visual comedy moment — the indignity of being physically placed on your own stage while trying to look natural is very Larry Sanders. 'Down you go' repeated is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Larry on stage: 'I know what you're thinking. Why... I should've taken you to Montana with me. I understand that. We could've all fit in the boat.'
jokes.setup: Larry's first words back on stage — the audience is cheering, emotional
jokes.punchline: Rather than acknowledging their love, he deflects by acknowledging their (presumed) complaint about being abandoned — and the 'we could've all fit in the boat' is a delightfully absurd specificity
jokes.explanation: A good monologue beat — Larry's inability to receive warmth gracefully is the show's central irony, and 'we could've all fit in the boat' is a charmingly specific absurdist detail that implies a very small boat.

jokes.text: Larry's painful on-air confession of 'drug addiction' — 'I had a... ahem... an addiction to painkillers... and then at times anti-anxiety medication and then later, of course, anything at all that came in a tablet or capsule form.'
jokes.setup: Larry has to publicly confirm the fake drug story to get his show back
jokes.punchline: The increasing specificity and escalation of his fake drug history — 'anything at all that came in a tablet or capsule form' — is both cringe and darkly funny, especially since we just watched him take actual pills backstage
jokes.explanation: The payoff on a long-running thread: Larry dismissed the drug story as pathetic, then took actual pills backstage, and now has to deliver the story publicly with escalating specificity. The dramatic irony is rich, and 'anything at all that came in a tablet or capsule form' is funny as a fake confession that accidentally sounds accurate.

jokes.text: Germain's assistant watching the confession: 'I had a feeling he was abusing his body in some way.' [oblivious to it being entirely fabricated]
jokes.setup: Larry is confessing to a completely fabricated drug problem on air
jokes.punchline: Germain's assistant watches with credulous conviction — 'I had a feeling' — proving the lie is more persuasive than the truth
jokes.explanation: A small but effective ironic beat — the credulous acceptance of the lie by someone who 'had a feeling' is a good jab at celebrity gossip culture.

jokes.text: 'Hi! Is Conan there?' [someone calling the show's phone line immediately after the confession]
jokes.setup: The emotional climax of Larry's public confession
jokes.punchline: Cut to a phone call — someone is trying to reach Conan O'Brien on Larry's line, underscoring Larry's ongoing irrelevance
jokes.explanation: A perfectly timed cut that undercuts the pathos of the confession. The Conan callback is set up earlier in the episode (the writer's offer) and pays off here. 'Hi! Is Conan there?' in this context is both very funny and a precise little industry-paranoia joke.

jokes.text: Artie watches the confession from backstage: 'Are you happy now?' Germain: 'Oh, yes!' And he'll mention it again at the end of the show? He will! And he'll MC the affiliates dinner in Kansas City? With great pleasure!'
jokes.setup: Larry is suffering through the humiliation of the fake confession
jokes.punchline: Germain is gleefully cataloguing all the additional humiliations Larry has signed up for — the MC gig in Kansas City is the escalating kicker
jokes.explanation: A good comedy-of-escalation — the price of getting the show back keeps growing, and Germain's glee is perfectly calibrated. 'Kansas City' is the specific detail that makes it funny.

jokes.text: Larry's monologue: 'Hillary Clinton got that new haircut. Yeah, she got that because that's how they're wearing it in prison.'
jokes.setup: Larry is doing his return monologue — a standard topical joke
jokes.punchline: The prison haircut implication is darker and more specific than expected
jokes.explanation: A functional but fairly standard political haircut joke of the era. The prison angle is edgier than expected but not exceptional. This is what a mid-5 joke looks like: it gets a chuckle but doesn't surprise.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I really don't care what they did before they were president.' [non-sequitur deflection after the Clinton joke]
jokes.setup: The Hillary Clinton prison joke has landed awkwardly
jokes.punchline: Larry's breezy 'I really don't care what they did before they were president' is a complete non-sequitur walk-back
jokes.explanation: A decent meta-comedy beat — Larry's monologue self-correction is very in character and suggests the joke didn't land as planned, which is itself funny.

jokes.text: 'I actually saw a hooker dressed in a Barney outfit. Now when Barney sings "you love me, I love you," it costs you 250 bucks.'
jokes.setup: Las Vegas is now family-friendly; Larry observed an odd sight
jokes.punchline: A prostitute in a Barney costume, charging $250 — the contrast of children's TV character and sex work is the joke
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed monologue joke — the Barney costume is a vivid, specific image and the $250 price point is oddly precise in a funny way. Standard monologue fare but executed well.

jokes.text: Larry backstage after the show: 'I can't believe it. These people actually love me MORE than they did before I had a drug problem.'
jokes.setup: Larry is processing the crowd's enthusiastic response to his fake confession
jokes.punchline: His amazement that a fabricated drug problem increased his popularity is both funny and a sharp satire of celebrity redemption culture
jokes.explanation: A sharp satirical observation that works as character comedy and cultural commentary simultaneously. The irony is rich: a FAKE drug problem makes Larry more beloved. This is exactly the kind of industry-insider insight the show excels at, and Larry's bewildered gratitude is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I got a great idea for sweeps week. Larry comes out and tells people he was molested as a child. Of course, we have people call your parents and tell them we're just making it up.'
jokes.setup: Larry is marveling at how much the fake drug story boosted his popularity
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately proposes escalating to a fake childhood molestation story — and the 'courtesy call to parents' detail is the peak of the darkness
jokes.explanation: One of the darkest and best jokes in the episode. The escalation from 'fake drug problem' to 'fake childhood molestation' is shocking enough, but the specific logistical detail of calling the parents to let them know it's fabricated is what makes it brilliant — it implies Artie has thought this through and is committed to production values even in the cover-up. It's a perfect encapsulation of Hollywood cynicism at its apex. Earns 8+ comfortably.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Still glad you came back from Montana?' Artie: 'I think if I learned one thing, it's that happiness comes from in here.' Artie: 'Is that your way of saying you'd like another pill?'
jokes.setup: Larry delivers a sincere-sounding lesson about inner happiness
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately reads it as a request for another pill — and is correct
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect closing joke. Larry's pseudo-profound 'happiness comes from in here' is immediately decoded by Artie as a pill request — and Larry confirms it with 'Yes, it is.' The joke is structurally immaculate: it delivers a fake emotional epiphany and then immediately demolishes it with pharmaceutical reality. The character integration is perfect — only these two characters in this specific dynamic could deliver this exchange. The rewatch bonus is significant: knowing the pill-passing earlier makes this land harder. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Bernadette Peters recites a poem for Larry — which turns out to be entirely about Hank Kingsley
jokes.setup: Bernadette builds up an emotional poem for Larry — 'the friend I could depend upon... but then one night I looked for him and found that he was gone'
jokes.punchline: 'Thank the lord, Hank Kingsley's back!' — the poem was never about Larry
jokes.explanation: The episode's finest comedic construction and its perfect closing joke. The poem is engineered to make the audience (and Larry) assume it's about Larry for its entire length — 'he was always there for me... found that he was gone... my friend returned' — and then the final line reveals it was always about Hank. The misdirection is sustained for a full minute of screen time, the reveal is maximally deflating for Larry's ego, and it ties together the episode's themes about Hank's importance and Larry's narcissistic blindspot. Structurally, this is as good as sitcom endings get. The joke also works as genuine satire: the universe where Hank gets the poem is the one where Larry's star power is properly contextualized. Earns its 8+ by a wide margin.

tmdb_overview: Larry's going out of his mind with boredom up in Montana when Artie appears with a scheme to resurrect the show.
